title: RBI Recurring Payment Rules: E-Mandate Limits (2026)
metaDescription: RBI's 2026 e-mandate rules: recurring card and UPI debits up to ₹15,000 need no extra authentication, ₹1 lakh for three categories, and a 24-hour notice.
h1: What are the RBI rules for recurring payments and e-mandates in 2026?
summary: The RBI's Digital Payments - E-mandate Framework, 2026, issued on April 21, 2026, sets the rules for recurring payments made with cards, prepaid instruments and UPI. Recurring debits up to ₹15,000 per transaction can go through without extra authentication once the first transaction is verified, and insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bill payments can go up to ₹1 lakh. The issuer must send a pre-transaction notice at least 24 hours before each debit, and you can withdraw a mandate at any time.

sections.heading: The current framework and what it replaced
paragraphs: The RBI's Digital Payments - E-mandate Framework, 2026 (reference RBI/DPSS/2026-27/396, dated April 21, 2026) is the rulebook for recurring transactions. It applies to payment system providers and participants processing recurring transactions, domestic or cross-border, using cards, prepaid payment instruments (PPI) or UPI.

The directions consolidate eight earlier RBI circulars and repeal them. Those run from the August 2019 card circular to the August 2024 circular that brought FASTag and NCMC top-ups into the framework. If you see a 2020 or 2021 notice cited in an older article, including the March 2021 extension of the compliance deadline, it is no longer the operative text. Use the 2026 directions as the reference.

sections.heading: Registration, the first payment and changes
paragraphs: A customer registers an e-mandate once. The mandate is registered only after the additional factor of authentication (AFA) is validated, on top of the bank's normal process. Every e-mandate carries a validity period, and the issuer must let you modify that period or withdraw the mandate at any point. Any change or withdrawal also needs AFA.

The first transaction under a mandate needs AFA. If it is processed together with registration, the two checks can be combined. Variable mandates let you set the maximum value of any recurring transaction. The directions also say no charges can be levied for the e-mandate facility, and that existing card mandates can be mapped to a reissued card.

sections.heading: How the limits changed
paragraphs: The ceiling for recurring card debits without AFA started at ₹2,000 per transaction under the August 2019 card circular, effective September 1, 2019. In December 2020 the RBI raised the AFA relaxation limit to ₹5,000 from January 1, 2021. In June 2022 it moved the limit to ₹15,000 per transaction.

On December 12, 2023, the RBI raised the limit from ₹15,000 to ₹1 lakh per transaction for three categories only: subscriptions to mutual funds, payment of insurance premiums and credit card bill payments. The 2026 directions carry both limits forward: ₹15,000 for all recurring transactions, and ₹1 lakh for those three categories.
list: Up to ₹15,000 per transaction: no AFA needed for subsequent recurring debits.
Above ₹15,000 (other than the three categories): AFA is needed for each transaction.
Insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bills: no AFA up to ₹1 lakh per transaction.

sections.heading: The 24-hour pre-transaction notice
paragraphs: The issuer must send a pre-transaction notification at least 24 hours before the actual debit. The notice must say, at a minimum, the merchant's name, the transaction amount, the date and time of debit, the e-mandate reference number, and the reason for the debit, which is the e-mandate you registered. You can choose or change the channel for the notice, such as SMS or email.

The notice gives you an opt-out. You can opt out of a particular transaction or of the whole e-mandate, and the opt-out is validated with AFA. FASTag and NCMC auto-replenishment mandates are exempt from the pre-transaction notice. After each debit, a post-transaction notice must follow, and it must include grievance redressal details.

sections.heading: Where bank pages and the rules disagree
paragraphs: Some bank help pages still describe older thresholds. HSBC's e-mandate FAQ, for example, describes authorising debits over ₹5,000, which matches the pre-2022 AFA limit rather than the current ₹15,000. Google Pay's help pages describe the ₹15,000 and ₹1 lakh thresholds, which match the directions.

The directions do not use the word pause. What they require is a facility to modify the validity period or withdraw the mandate. If your app offers a pause, that is a feature of the app, and it does not change your rights under the RBI rules.

sections.heading: What to do with this as a customer
paragraphs: When a recurring debit is due, check the pre-transaction notice against the mandate you approved. If the amount is above ₹15,000 and is not one of the three higher-limit categories, expect an authentication prompt on the due date. If a debit is wrong, raise it with your issuer's grievance channel first, since the directions require a dispute redressal system and apply the RBI's customer liability rules to e-mandates.
Keep a list of your active mandates with the validity end date for each. Essara's UPI AutoPay tracker can hold that list, but you enter each mandate yourself.

faqs.q: What is the RBI limit for UPI AutoPay without a UPI PIN?
faqs.a: Under the 2026 directions, recurring transactions up to ₹15,000 per transaction can be authorised without AFA. Google Pay's help page describes the same threshold: if a mandate amount is below ₹15,000, you enter your UPI PIN for the first payment, and for larger amounts you enter it when each payment is due.

faqs.q: Does the ₹1 lakh limit apply to EMIs and loan repayments?
faqs.a: The directions name only three categories for the ₹1 lakh limit: insurance premiums, mutual fund subscriptions and credit card bill payments. Other recurring debits above ₹15,000 need authentication. Check your lender's terms for how EMIs are collected.

faqs.q: Will my bank send a notice before every recurring debit?
faqs.a: The directions require a pre-transaction notice at least 24 hours before each debit. The exceptions are FASTag and NCMC auto-replenishment, which have no fixed schedule. If you do not receive a notice for a covered debit, report it to your issuer.

faqs.q: Can I stop a recurring payment after the RBI rules?
faqs.a: Yes. The issuer must provide a facility to withdraw any e-mandate at any point, and withdrawal needs AFA validation. Cancel in the card issuer's or UPI app's mandate section, and also cancel the subscription with the merchant.

faqs.q: Does the e-mandate framework cover NACH debits?
faqs.a: The 2026 directions apply to recurring transactions using cards, PPI and UPI, and they do not name NACH. Notice and cancellation rules for NACH mandates come from NPCI and your bank, so confirm them with your bank.

faqs.q: Why does my bank app still mention ₹5,000?
faqs.a: Some bank help pages were written under the older AFA limit of ₹5,000, which was raised to ₹15,000 in June 2022. The RBI's current directions are the reference.
